paragraphs.heading: What a core sample is
paragraphs.text: A core sample is a cylinder-shaped section of some substance, usually a naturally occurring one. Most are obtained by drilling into sediment, rock or another substance with a hollow steel tube known as a core drill. During coring the sample is forced into the tube more or less intact. In the laboratory it is taken out of the tube, inspected and analyzed, with the techniques chosen according to the kind of data wanted.

paragraphs.heading: A wide range of sizes
paragraphs.text: The diameter of a core can be as little as a few millimeters, in wood, or more than 150 millimeters, which is routine in oil exploration. Lengths run from less than a meter up to around 200 meters in a single run. The materials sampled vary from almost liquid to the strongest found in nature or technology. A core can come from a laboratory bench or from more than 10 km from the Earth's surface, down a borehole.

paragraphs.heading: Dropping, shaking and drilling
paragraphs.text: A variety of core samplers exist for different materials and conditions. In gravity coring, the sampler is dropped into the material, usually the bed of a body of water. This technique is common in geological studies of recent aquatic deposits, and because the materials it goes through are weak, the cores have to be relatively small. In vibrating, the sampler is vibrated so that it can penetrate. In drilling, a rotating ring-shaped tool is pressed against the material to cut out a cylinder of it.

paragraphs.heading: Coring by hand
paragraphs.text: Coring can also be done by hand. The tool may be a Russian Peat Corer, a piston corer held in the hand, or just a hollow tube. The advantages are low cost and quick operation. The drawback is depth. A handheld corer reaches only limited depths: a few decimeters where the soil is clay, and a few meters in the soft sediments of a lake.

paragraphs.heading: Damage along the way
paragraphs.text: The mechanical forces a tool puts on a core frequently fracture it, and some intervals can be lost. This can greatly complicate the interpretation of the core. Core samples also always degrade to some degree while they are being cut, handled and studied. More attention and care is now being put into preventing damage during transport and analysis. The usual way is to freeze the core completely with liquid nitrogen, and in some cases special polymers are used to preserve and cushion it.

paragraphs.heading: Why context matters
paragraphs.text: A core that cannot be related to where it was before it was taken has lost much of its benefit. The identity of the borehole, and the position and orientation of the core within it, meaning which way up it was, are critical. If these data become separated from the core, it is generally impossible to get them back. This is true even for a core taken from a tree trunk. Dendrochronologists always aim to keep a bark surface in the sample, so that the date of the tree's most recent growth can be determined without doubt.
